title: Objection! — your EU Law exam topics

items.text: A service within the meaning of Art 56 TFEU involves a non-tangible performance that is normally provided for remuneration and is of a temporary nature.
items.ground: The model answer explicitly states this definition and applies it to remote medical consultations, showing that such services fall within the scope of Art 56 TFEU.
items.why: The model answer uses this definition to establish that MediLink's remote medical consultations qualify as services under Art 56 TFEU, which is necessary for applying the free movement rules.

items.text: A service under Art 56 TFEU must involve a tangible performance that is provided for free, not for remuneration.
items.ground: The model answer explicitly states this definition and applies it to remote medical consultations, showing that such services fall within the scope of Art 56 TFEU.
items.why: The model answer uses this definition to establish that MediLink's remote medical consultations qualify as services under Art 56 TFEU, which is necessary for applying the free movement rules.

items.text: Restrictions to the freedom to provide services can be justified on the basis of imperative requirements in the public interest under Article 52 TFEU.
items.ground: The model answer explicitly cites Gebhard and Laval as examples of cases where such justifications were accepted, and applies this principle to the Slovenian law.
items.why: The model answer argues that the Slovenian law's objective of protecting public health constitutes a valid justification under Article 52 TFEU, which is a key principle for assessing the legality of restrictions.

items.text: Article 52 TFEU only allows restrictions to be justified if they are necessary and proportionate to the objective pursued, not simply because they relate to public interest.
items.ground: The model answer explicitly cites Gebhard and Laval as examples of cases where such justifications were accepted, and applies this principle to the Slovenian law.
items.why: The model answer argues that the Slovenian law's objective of protecting public health constitutes a valid justification under Article 52 TFEU, which is a key principle for assessing the legality of restrictions.

items.text: Article 101 TFEU applies to agreements or concerted practices that restrict competition, regardless of whether they are formal written contracts.
items.ground: The functional definition of an undertaking includes any entity engaged in economic activity, and cooperation can take the form of concerted practice without requiring a formal agreement.
items.why: The law recognizes that cooperation in the form of public statements of support can constitute a concerted practice under Article 101 TFEU, even without a written agreement.

items.text: Article 101 TFEU only applies to formal written agreements between undertakings, not to informal cooperation or public statements of support.
items.ground: The functional definition of an undertaking includes any entity engaged in economic activity, and cooperation can take the form of concerted practice without requiring a formal agreement.
items.why: The law recognizes that cooperation in the form of public statements of support can constitute a concerted practice under Article 101 TFEU, even without a written agreement.

items.text: Article 107 TFEU applies to state aid that distorts or threatens to distort competition by favouring certain undertakings.
items.ground: State aid is defined as any advantage granted by a member state or through state resources that distorts competition, and the municipality's actions involve financial benefits to specific undertakings.
items.why: The municipality's actions involve financial benefits such as reduced municipal charges, lower interest rates, and commitment to purchase services, which constitute state aid under EU law.

items.text: Article 107 TFEU only applies to aid granted by the European Commission, not to municipal actions that provide financial benefits to companies.
items.ground: State aid is defined as any advantage granted by a member state or through state resources that distorts competition, and the municipality's actions involve financial benefits to specific undertakings.
items.why: The municipality's actions involve financial benefits such as reduced municipal charges, lower interest rates, and commitment to purchase services, which constitute state aid under EU law.

items.text: Article 101 TFEU requires either restrictive object or restrictive effect to be established for an agreement to be prohibited.
items.ground: The Court of Justice has established that object and effect are alternative elements, with object being sufficient to establish prohibition without requiring detailed effects analysis.
items.why: In cases where the object of an agreement is inherently restrictive, such as a pause in frontier AI development, the restrictive effect need not be proven if the object is clearly anticompetitive.

items.text: Article 101 TFEU only prohibits agreements that have a restrictive effect on competition, regardless of whether they have a restrictive object.
items.ground: The Court of Justice has established that object and effect are alternative elements, with object being sufficient to establish prohibition without requiring detailed effects analysis.
items.why: In cases where the object of an agreement is inherently restrictive, such as a pause in frontier AI development, the restrictive effect need not be proven if the object is clearly anticompetitive.

items.text: A non-privileged applicant challenging a legislative act must establish that it is both directly and individually concerned by that act.
items.ground: This follows from the case law interpreting Article 263(4) TFEU, particularly in relation to the 'direct concern' and 'individual concern' tests.
items.why: The Court has consistently held that for a non-privileged applicant to have standing to challenge a legislative act, it must show both direct and individual concern under the Plaumann test.

items.text: A non-privileged applicant can challenge a legislative act if it is only directly concerned, without needing to prove individual concern.
items.ground: This follows from the case law interpreting Article 263(4) TFEU, particularly in relation to the 'direct concern' and 'individual concern' tests.
items.why: The Court has consistently held that for a non-privileged applicant to have standing to challenge a legislative act, it must show both direct and individual concern under the Plaumann test.

items.text: National courts may annul national sanctions imposed by authorities if those sanctions are disproportionate, even if they cannot annul the EU act that forms their basis.
items.ground: This is supported by the principle that national courts can review the proportionality of national measures under EU law, as long as they do not invalidate EU acts directly.
items.why: The national court can assess whether the fine imposed is disproportionate under EU principles, but cannot directly annul the EU act that sets the threshold, as that would require a preliminary reference.

items.text: National courts may not annul national sanctions based on disproportionate application of EU law, as they are bound by the validity of EU acts.
items.ground: This is supported by the principle that national courts can review the proportionality of national measures under EU law, as long as they do not invalidate EU acts directly.
